(a) Morley-Minto Reforms (1909) and the partition of Bengal — both of which created a choice between constitutional engagement and revolutionary protest
(b) Government of India Act 1935 and the provincial elections of 1937 — the question of whether Congress should form governments in reformed provincial legislatures
(c) Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919) and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre — reforming the same government that had simultaneously ordered colonial brutality
(d) Communal Award (1932) and the Gandhi-Irwin Pact — the question of whether to accept separate electorates as the price of constitutional progress

solution.concept_anchor: Indian members of Hunter Commission minority report
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) naming Sultan Ahmed is deceptive because he is among the less well-known of the Indian minority report members, and students uncertain about him may suspect he doesn't belong.
elimination_logic: Identify the category: Indian members who formed the minority report of the Hunter (Disorders Inquiry) Commission.
Jagat Narayan, C.H. Setalvad, and Sultan Ahmed were the three Indian members who jointly signed the minority report — all three belong.
Verify Srinivasa Iyengar: he was a Congress leader of the period but was not a member of the Hunter Commission.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The composition of the Hunter Commission's Indian minority is a specific factual area that rewards precise study. Students who know the minority report was signed by Indian members but cannot name them individually will guess based on which name sounds most plausible for a 1920 legal/political figure. Srinivasa Iyengar was a prominent Congress leader of the period — his name is plausible enough to deceive students without precise knowledge of the Commission's actual composition.
solution.final_explanation:
The Hunter Commission had both British majority members and Indian minority members, and the two groups produced drastically different reports.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because both A and R are correct and students who know that Gandhi's arrest caused crowd anger will assume the causal link runs exactly as R describes — but the causal chain is more complex than R states.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Gandhi was arrested near Delhi on 8 April 1919 while attempting to travel to Punjab, and this arrest preceded the violent outbreaks in Amritsar and Ahmedabad.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Gandhi had called for the hartal on 6 April as a specific response to the passage of the Rowlatt Act.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. R explains why Gandhi called the hartal, not why his arrest triggered violence. The causal link between Gandhi's arrest and the violent crowd response is explained by the sudden removal of leadership and the psychological effect of the state suppressing the movement's leader — not by the hartal call itself. R explains A's predecessor event but not the specific causal mechanism that A describes.
Both A and R are correct but R does not explain A — correct option is (b).
solution.final_explanation:
Gandhi's arrest on 8 April 1919 near Delhi was a pivotal event in the sequence leading to violence across Punjab and in Ahmedabad.

Assertion (A) analysis: Correct. Gandhi was detained by British authorities near Delhi while attempting to reach Punjab, where the Rowlatt Act agitation was most intense. His arrest occurred on 8 April — two days after the hartal — and the violent outbreaks in Amritsar (killing of Europeans) and Ahmedabad (burning of buildings) followed thereafter.

Reason (R) analysis: Correct. Gandhi had called the hartal specifically as a protest against the Rowlatt Act's passage — this is accurate and well-documented.

Causal relationship: R does not explain A. R explains the reason for the hartal call (6 April) but does not explain why Gandhi's arrest on 8 April triggered violent responses. The arrest-to-violence link is mediated by the psychological effect of leadership removal — a leaderless crowd responding to state suppression — not by the hartal call's purpose.

Value Addition:
• Gandhi's arrest was the British authorities' pre-emptive attempt to prevent him from reaching Punjab and amplifying the agitation.
• The violence that followed was used by Dyer and O'Dwyer to justify martial law — creating a chain where the state's own action (arrest) contributed to the conditions it then claimed to be controlling.

solution.final_explanation:
The Jallianwala Bagh National Memorial has both a statutory history and a contemporary diplomatic dimension.

statement_analysis.reason: Ataturk's abolition of the Caliphate in 1924 fundamentally undermined the Khilafat Movement's purpose — once the Caliphate itself no longer existed, there was no institution to defend, leading to the movement's rapid decline.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) claiming all four are correct is deceptive because Statement 2 is incorrect, but it contains a plausible-sounding description of the chronology that rewards imprecise knowledge.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 2: the Khilafat Movement's cause was the Ottoman Caliphate, not the Rowlatt Act — Gandhi linked them tactically but they were distinct causes. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Verify Statements 1, 3, and 4: all three are accurate descriptions of documented historical facts.
Three statements (1, 3, 4) are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the Khilafat-Rowlatt conflation that is among the most common errors on this topic. Students who know Gandhi linked both causes assume they originated together or that one caused the other. The Khilafat Movement had an entirely independent origin — post-WWI British policy on Turkey — and was a separate religious-political agitation that Gandhi chose to support simultaneously with the anti-Rowlatt agitation. The linkage was Gandhi's strategic choice, not a causal connection.
solution.final_explanation:
The Khilafat-Non-Cooperation nexus requires careful understanding of causes, connections, and outcomes.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Gandhi explicitly cited Punjab wrongs (Jallianwala Bagh and martial law) and the Khilafat issue as the twin planks of the Non-Cooperation Movement — both are documented in his speeches and the Congress's formal resolutions.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Khilafat Movement was not triggered by the Rowlatt Act. It arose from post-WWI British policy on the Ottoman Empire and the anticipated dismemberment of Turkey. Gandhi linked both causes tactically, but their origins were independent.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The 1919 Rowlatt Act protests did see Hindu-Muslim joint participation — a cross-communal unity that predated the formal Khilafat-Congress alliance and which Gandhi sought to institutionalise.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Ataturk's abolition of the Ottoman Caliphate in 1924 removed the Khilafat Movement's entire raison d'être, contributing to its rapid collapse and the subsequent communal tensions in India.

Value Addition:
• The Ali brothers (Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali) led the Khilafat Committee alongside their Congress cooperation.
• The post-Khilafat period saw rising communal tensions — the Hindu-Muslim unity of 1919-20 was relatively brief.
• Gandhi's decision to support the Khilafat cause remains one of the most debated tactical decisions of his political career.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) claiming 1919 is deceptive because the Rowlatt Act was passed in 1919 and students may confuse the year of passage with the year of repeal, especially since the Act was never used.

solution.final_explanation:
The Rowlatt Act, despite generating enormous political agitation, was never used against any individual and was ultimately repealed.

• Option (b) — 1919: Incorrect. This was the year of the Act's passage, not its repeal. Confusing year of enactment with year of repeal is a common error.
• Option (c) — 1922: Correct. The Rowlatt Act was repealed in 1922 — after the Non-Cooperation Movement. Its repeal came as a political concession following sustained mass agitation, even though the Act had never been operationally deployed.
• Option (d) — 1935: Incorrect. 1935 is the year of the Government of India Act — entirely different legislation from a different era.

Value Addition:
• The Act was repealed without ever being used — making it perhaps the most consequential unused legislation in Indian colonial history.
• Its repeal was one of Gandhi's explicit demands when launching Non-Cooperation — alongside redress of Punjab wrongs and Khilafat grievances.
• The political and symbolic weight of an unenforceable statute whose mere existence triggered mass revolution is a remarkable historical phenomenon.

statement_analysis.reason: Dyer's own testimony before the Hunter Commission stated his intent was to produce a moral and deterrent effect throughout Punjab, not simply to disperse a local crowd — this admission was central to the Commission's deliberations and to the minority report's condemnation.

statement_analysis.reason: Dyer's own testimony confirmed that firing stopped only when ammunition was exhausted — not when the crowd dispersed, and no warning was given before firing began.

statement_analysis.reason: The majority report characterised Dyer's actions as an 'error of judgment' rather than a deliberate massacre and explicitly did not recommend criminal prosecution — only the Indian minority report was more condemnatory.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 inverts the Hunter Commission majority report's conclusion. Students who know the Commission was 'critical of Dyer' may assume this criticism extended to recommending criminal prosecution. The majority report's 'error of judgment' framing was itself a politically significant choice — it criticised Dyer but insulated him from criminal accountability. Only the Indian minority report advocated stronger action.
solution.final_explanation:
General Dyer's own testimony before the Hunter Commission was remarkably self-incriminating.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Dyer stated his aim was not simply dispersing the Amritsar crowd but producing a 'moral effect' across Punjab — signalling that mass killing would be the consequence of continued unrest. This admission transformed the legal and moral analysis from proportionate crowd control to punitive deterrence.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The 1,650 rounds were fired without warning and stopped only when ammunition was exhausted — not when the crowd had dispersed or when an evacuation route was provided. This firing pattern was central to the minority report's condemnation.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Hunter Commission majority report described Dyer's action as an 'error of judgment' — not a 'deliberate massacre.' It did not recommend criminal prosecution, only administrative action. The framing was a political compromise that satisfied neither Indian nor liberal British opinion.

Value Addition:
• The absence of a warning order before firing was explicitly noted by the Hunter Commission as a grave irregularity.
• Dyer's 'moral effect' testimony is among the most quoted statements in colonial history — it is a primary source that remains central to historiographical debates.
• The gap between Dyer's admitted intent and the majority report's 'error of judgment' conclusion reveals the political constraints on colonial accountability mechanisms.

formatted_presentation.display_text:
Consider the following statements about the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and its official investigation:

1. General Dyer testified before the Hunter Commission that his purpose at Jallianwala Bagh was not merely to disperse the crowd but to produce a 'moral effect' across Punjab — an admission that directly undermined any claim of proportionate crowd control.
2. The firing at Jallianwala Bagh continued until all 1,650 rounds of ammunition were exhausted — it did not stop when the crowd had dispersed or when an escape route was cleared.
3. The Hunter Commission's majority report concluded that Dyer's actions constituted a deliberate massacre and recommended his criminal prosecution under the Indian Penal Code.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?

(a) 1 and 2 only
(b) 2 and 3 only
(c) 1 and 3 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3
